coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound chain: growth without profit, negative unit economics, a weak pop-up, a broken runway, then the software alternative. X states the founders' hypothesis up front, breaks it into six conditions and uses that table as the spine of the deck, so each section answers one named condition. Its executive summary carries the key numbers and maps one-to-one onto the sections. Y is also well ordered, with section summary slides and action titles, but its executive summary is thinner on numbers and the argument is spread over more slides. Y's acquisition-bill detour ($13.7M) adds a branch that the governing thought does not need. X is somewhat tighter from governing thought down to evidence.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: do not launch, grow the software business, and sell store-based fast delivery to grocers. X weighs the alternatives better. It constructs and rejects a one-store pilot, showing that it loses about $2M a year, breaches the runway in month 10 and adds little learning; this is the key's 'learning from a test vs consuming runway' trade-off and its trap of launching in one city to prove density. X also tells the board not to extend the pop-up, phases hires in tranches against signed contracts, sets a 90-day checkpoint and gives a 34% growth threshold below which its own recommendation fails. Y never considers a pilot or capped test; its excluded branches are a new round, rivals and other cities. Y does add a useful channel-conflict point (an own service would turn pipeline grocers into rivals) and a risk table with owners. Its stress test of the software path is thinner, limited to 60% versus 30% growth.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: −$6.17 at the median, −$1.76 at best observed, −$12.57 for the pop-up, $2.5M and about six months of runway at month 18, and −$1.05 with Zipcart's moves. X also gives the CAGR explicitly (41.5%), break-even AOV at both the median ($63) and the best observed case ($50), the break-even density under Zipcart's moves (1,042 orders a day), and a scale check showing the plan implies $266M of sales, more than QuickBasket's total revenue. Y adds the −$0.48 no-volume-loss case, single-lever break-evens (14.4 orders per rider-hour) and a rider-pay sensitivity; all are correct. X's weaknesses: its single-driver sensitivity chart appears to have mislabelled bars (the riders and density values are swapped against the labels), though the title and text state the right conclusion. 'Top-quartile density' is not supported by the pack, and its monthly cash model rests on several constructed assumptions, which it flags. Y's weaknesses: the $13.7M 'acquisition bill' is a rough steady-state estimate that carries the strong claim 'density cannot be bought'. 'Without either, the plan loses about $0.30' understates the AOV case, which is −$0.73. It gives only year-on-year growth, not the CAGR. Overall X uses the critical evidence a little more fully, but the gap is small.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis, as the key expects, and neither treats market growth or the 18% weekly pop-up growth as validation. X handles it more explicitly and more fairly. It names the hypothesis, tests six necessary conditions, and reverses it. It still grants the pop-up's 'fair caveat: it was early', and concedes from the Zipcart evidence that 'a profitable route may exist' at high density with premium pricing. It turns that concession into a re-entry trigger: a service fee that works without losing more than 15% of volume. Y credits the founders on growth and takes Zipcart apart well as a price rise rather than an operating gain. But it is more dismissive of the partial support, and its re-entry tests do not include the fee route.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong, reach the defensible conclusion and avoid every major trap. X serves the board better for four reasons. It tests the founders' case condition by condition. It closes off the tempting middle option, a one-store pilot or an extended pop-up, with numbers. It shows the runway breach under both readings of the $9.5M with a monthly cash view. And it states the 34% growth threshold at which its own software recommendation would fail, with phased hires and a 90-day checkpoint. Y's additions are worthwhile: the channel-conflict argument, the rider-pay sensitivity and the −$0.48 Zipcart case. But Y is longer, omits the pilot alternative, and leans on a speculative acquisition-cost estimate. X's mislabelled sensitivity chart is a blemish that does not affect its conclusions.
